                                                               The convergence rate of p-harmonic
                                                                 to infinity-harmonic functions




arXiv:2302.08462v2 [math.AP] 10 Oct 2023
                                                                                       Leon Bungert∗
                                                                                     October 11, 2023


                                                                                           Abstract
                                                     The purpose of this paper is to prove a uniform convergence rate of the solutions of
                                                 the p-Laplace equation ∆p u = 0 with Dirichlet boundary conditions to the solution of
                                                 the infinity-Laplace equation ∆∞ u = 0 as p → ∞. The rate scales like p− /4 for general
                                                                                                                               1

                                                                                               −1/2
                                                 solutions of the Dirichlet problem and like p      for solutions with positive gradient. An
                                                 explicit example shows that it cannot be better than p−1 . The proof of this result solely
                                                 relies on the comparison principle with the fundamental solutions of the p-Laplace and the
                                                 infinity-Laplace equation, respectively. Our argument does not use viscosity solutions, is
                                                 purely metric, and is therefore generalizable to more general settings where a comparison
                                                 principle with Hölder cones and Hölder regularity is available.
                                                 Keywords: p-Laplacian, infinity-Laplacian, convergence rates, comparison principle
                                                 AMS subject classifications: 26A16, 35B51, 35D30, 35D40, 35J92, 35J94


                                           1     Introduction
                                           The infinity-Laplace equation first appeared in [38] as optimality condition for absolutely mini-
                                           mizing Lipschitz extensions. There it was formally derived as the limit equation of p-Laplacian
                                           problems of the form
                                                                                (
                                                                                  ∆p u = 0      in Ω,
                                                                                                                                       (1.1)
                                                                                  u = gp        on ∂Ω,

                                                                                                                                             p−2
                                           where the p-Laplace operator of a smooth function u is defined as ∆p u := div(|∇u| ∇u),
                                           Ω ⊂ Rd is a bounded domain, and gp : ∂Ω → R is some boundary datum. To derive the
                                           infinity-Laplace equation, one expands the p-Laplacian as
                                                                                                              
                                                                            p−4      2
                                                                ∆p u = |∇u|      |∇u| ∆u + (p − 2)h∇u, D2 u ∇ui .             (1.2)

                                           Using the homogeneity of the equation (1.1) and carelessly dividing by |∇u|, the right limit
                                           equation as p → ∞ turns out to be
                                                                             (
                                                                               ∆∞ u = 0     in Ω,
                                                                                                                                  (1.3)
                                                                               u = g∞       on ∂Ω,
                                              ∗ Institute of Mathematics, University of Würzburg, Emil-Fischer-Str. 40, 97074 Würzburg, Germany. Email:

                                           leon.bungert@uni-wuerzburg.de


                                                                                                1
where the infinity-Laplace operator is defined as ∆∞ u := h∇u, D2 u ∇ui, and g∞ : ∂Ω → R is a
Lipschitz continuous boundary datum. One can make this limit rigorous using the framework
or viscosity solutions, see, e.g., [14, 27]. Alternatively, one can consider a variational limit of
the p-Laplacian problems, given by the absolutely minimizing Lipschitz extension problem:
                       (
                         Lip(u; U ) = Lip(u; ∂U )     ∀ subdomains U ⊂ Ω,
                                                                                              (1.4)
                         u = g∞                       on ∂Ω.

Here Lip(u; X) := supx,y∈X |u(x)−u(y)|
                                   |x−y|   is the Lipschitz constant of u on X ⊂ Ω. While in
Euclidean space (1.3) is equivalent to (1.4) (see [27]), the latter formulation can be extended to
more general settings like graphs [4, 6, 25] or length spaces [26, 30], where a PDE like (1.3) might
not be available. Yet another equivalent formulation of (1.3) and (1.4) is the “comparison with
cones” principle [27]. It states that a function solves these two problems if and only if it admits
a comparison principle with cone functions of the form x 7→ a |x − x0 | + b. While the necessity
of this property is not really surprising (given that all solutions of the p-Laplace equation (1.1)
                                                                                           p−d
for p > d also admit a comparison principle with functions of the form x 7→ a |x − x0 | p−1 + b)
the sufficiency is an astonishing feature of the infinity-Laplace equation (1.3).
    Building upon the theory developed for this equation, an extensive body of literature has
formed around other infinity-Laplacian type problems which arise as p-Laplacian limits. For
instance, one should mention the eigenvalue problem [5, 15, 16, 32], vector-valued problems
[20, 21], problems with gradient constraints and limits of p-Poisson equations [2, 13, 34], and
infinity-harmonic potentials [1, 10], where the list of references is far from being complete.
    The present paper focuses on the standard infinity-Laplace equation (1.3) and shall answer
a question which appears to be entirely unexplored in the literature:
   How fast do the solutions of the p-Laplace equation (1.1) converge to the solution of the
                          infinity-Laplace equation (1.3) as p → ∞?
The answer to this question was already revealed in the abstract and reads: At least as fast as
p−1/4 tends to zero. In certain scenarios the rate can be improved to p−1/2 but it can never be
better than p−1 , which is the convergence rate of the fundamental solutions to the p-Laplace
equation to the one of the infinity-Laplace equation.
    Most related to the present work are our papers [3, 4] in collaboration with Jeff Calder and
Tim Roith. There we used the “comparison with cones” property of infinity-harmonic func-
tions together with techniques from [17, 23] to prove rates of convergence for infinity-harmonic
functions on sparse geometric graphs as the graph approximates a continuum. Furthermore,
in [17, 23] the convergence rate for solutions of the inhomogeneous infinity Laplace equation
−∆∞ u = γ as γ ց 0 was proven to be at most γ 1/3 .
    Our key insight in [3, 4] was that graph infinity-harmonic functions satisfy a comparison
principle with respect to functions that are close to a Euclidean cone, which enabled us to prove
rates of convergence to an infinity-harmonic function. In more detail, in [4] we utilize explicit
error estimates between distance functions on a geometric graph and Euclidean cone functions
to prove the rates. In [3] we use percolation theory to show that ratios of graph distances on
sparse graphs converge to the corresponding ratio of Euclidean distances which is also sufficient
for proving rates. In the present paper, we transfer this line of thought to solutions of the
p-Laplace equation for large p and prove rates of convergence using explicit error estimates
                                           p−d
between ratios of Hölder cones x 7→ |x| p−1 and the ratios of Euclidean (or Lipschitz) cones
x 7→ |x|.
    The rest of the paper is organized as follows: In Section 2 we introduce our notation, recap
the concepts of solutions and comparison principles for equations (1.1) and (1.3), state our

                                                 2
main result, and discuss some extensions to the fractional infinity-Laplacian and equations
on metric measure spaces. Section 3 is devoted to its proof: In Section 3.1 we first recap
important connections between infinity-harmonic functions and sub- and supersolutions of a
finite difference infinity-Laplacian, as well as some perturbation results. In Section 3.2 we prove
an approximate sub- and supersolution property for p-harmonic functions with large values of p
which is key for proving the rates in Section 3.3.


2     Setting and main result
2.1    Notation
In this paper we assume that Ω ⊂ Rd is an open domain, we do not pose any regularity assump-
tions on its boundary. With Lp (Ω) and W1,p (Ω) for p ∈ [1, ∞] we denote standard Lebesgue
and Sobolev spaces, equipped with the norms k·kLp and k·kW1,p , respectively. Furthermore,
for p ∈ [1, ∞) the space W01,p (Ω) is defined as the closure of the space of compactly supported
smooth functions with respect to the norm k·kW1,p .
    The space of continuous functions on Ω is denoted by C(Ω) and equipped with the supremal
norm kuk∞ := supΩ |u|. With C0,α (Ω) for α ∈ (0, 1] we denote the space of α-Hölder continuous
functions, equipped with the norm kuk0,α := kuk∞ + [u]0,α , where the Hölder semi-norm is
defined as
                                                                        
                                        |u(x) − u(y)|
                       [u]0,α := sup              α    : x, y ∈ Ω, x 6= y .
                                           |x − y|

For d < p < ∞ the Sobolev spaces W01,p (Ω) are continuously embedded in the Hölder spaces
C0,1−d/p (Ω), see [28, Theorem 4.12].

2.2    Solutions of the p-Laplace and infinity-Laplace equations
We continue with defining solutions of the p-Laplace equation (1.1) and the infinity-Laplace
equation (1.3).
Definition 2.1. Let p > d and gp ∈ W1,p (Ω) ∩ C(Ω). We say that up ∈ W1,p (Ω) ∩ C(Ω) solves
(1.1) if up = gp on ∂Ω and
               Z              Z
                        p           p
                  |∇up | dx ≤   |∇v| dx     ∀v ∈ W1,p (Ω) : v − gp ∈ W01,p (Ω).
               Ω                Ω

Definition 2.2. Let g∞ ∈ W1,∞ (Ω) ∩ C(Ω). We say that u∞ ∈ C(Ω) solves (1.3) if it is a
viscosity solution of (1.3).
Remark 2.1 (Existence and uniqueness). Existence and uniqueness of solutions in the above
sense are classical results. For solutions of the p-Laplace equation in the sense of Definition 2.1
we refer to [12, Theorem 2.16, Section 3.1]. As explained therein, the boundary of the domain
can be arbitrarily irregular since we assume that the boundary data are continuous on Ω and
that p > d. For an existence proof of solutions to the infinity-Laplace equation, constructed as
limits of p-Laplacian solutions we refer to [14, Theorem 4.6]. Uniqueness was proved with quite
different methods in [22, 31, 33].
   Our analysis is entirely based upon the comparison principle of p-harmonic and infinity-
harmonic functions with the respective fundamental solutions.


                                                3
Proposition 2.1. Let up solve (1.1) for d < p < ∞ or (1.3) for p = ∞. Furthermore, define
the function
                                      (         p−d
                                        |x − y| p−1 , if p < ∞,
                         dp (x, y) :=
                                        |x − y| ,     if p = ∞.

Then for all domains D ⋐ Ω, compactly contained in Ω, for all a ≥ 0, and for all x0 ∈ Rd \ D
it holds

      min {u(ξ) − a dp (ξ, x0 )} ≤ u(x) − a dp (x, x0 ) ≤ max {u(ξ) − a dp (ξ, x0 )} ,        ∀x ∈ D.
      ξ∈∂D                                                  ξ∈∂D

Proof. See [36] for p < ∞ and [14, Proposition 6.2] or [27] for p = ∞.
Remark 2.2. The astonishing property of infinity-harmonic functions is that they are charac-
terized through the comparison principle from Proposition 2.1, see [27]. This is not the case
for p-harmonic functions, however, the comparison principle alone turns out to be enough.

2.3    Main result
The following theorem is our main result and provides a convergence rate which depends on
the Hölder-regularity of the p-harmonic functions up (which, a-priori, are at least 1 − d/p-Hölder
continuous).
Theorem 1 (Explicit convergence rate). Let up ∈ W1,p (Ω) solve (1.1) for p > d and u∞ ∈
W1,∞ (Ω) solve (1.3). Assume that up ∈ C0,αp (Ω) for some αp ∈ [1 − d/p, 1], and that

                                     H := lim sup [up ]0,αp < ∞.
                                            p→∞

Then there exists a constant C(Ω, H, ku∞ k0,1 ) ∈ (0, ∞) such that for all p > d sufficiently large
it holds that
                                                        αp
                                                   d − 1 2αp +2
              kup − u∞ k∞ ≤ C(Ω, H, ku∞ k0,1 )                  + max |gp − g∞ | .
                                                   p−1              ∂Ω

If ess inf Ω |∇u∞ | =: γ > 0, then this can be improved to
                                                                 α2p
                                  C(Ω, H, ku∞ k0,1 )       d−1
                 kup − u∞ k∞ ≤                                           + max |gp − g∞ | .
                                           γ2              p−1              ∂Ω

   A couple of remarks on Theorem 1 are in order.
Remark 2.3 (Boundary term). Since we are considering uniform convergence rates, measures
through the supremal norm on Ω, the rate has to be dominated by the convergence rate of
the boundary data, which explains the term max∂Ω |gp − g∞ |. Hence, the only interesting case
is that the boundary data coincide, or converge quicker than the first term, such that the
boundary term has no bearing.
Remark 2.4 (Asymptotic rate). Let us now assume gp = g∞ for simplicity. Since αp → 1
as p → ∞, for large values of p the convergence rates all behave like the rate for Lipschitz
regularity with αp = 1. It holds
                                                             1
                                    lim sup kup − u∞ k∞ p 4 < ∞
                                     p→∞



                                                  4
and if ess inf Ω |∇u∞ | > 0 then
                                                                 1
                                   lim sup kup − u∞ k∞ p 2 < ∞.
                                    p→∞

This justifies the claim from the abstract of this paper which states that the convergence rate
scales like p−1/4 , respectively p−1/2 in the second case.
Remark 2.5 (The assumption H < ∞). Without any prior knowledge on the Hölder regularity
of up , besides the trivial C0,1−d/p regularity, one can apply Morrey’s inequality for αp = 1 − d/p
to vp := up − gp ∈ W01,p (Ω) (see [14, Lemma 2.3]) to get

                                                   2pd
                                    [vp ]0,αp ≤        k∇vp kLp .
                                                  p−d
Taking the lim sup as p → ∞ we obtain, using also Definition 2.1, that
                                                                                      
             lim sup [vp ]0,αp ≤ 2 lim sup k∇vp kLp ≤ 2 lim sup k∇up kLp + k∇gp kLp
              p→∞                  p→∞                           p→∞

                             ≤ 4 lim sup k∇gp kLp .
                                   p→∞

This implies that
                                                                                        
     H = lim sup [up ]0,αp ≤ lim sup [vp ]0,αp + [gp ]0,αp ≤ lim sup 4 k∇gp kLp + [gp ]0,αp ,
           p→∞                p→∞                                      p→∞

meaning that a uniform bound on semi-norms of the boundary data imply a uniform bound on
the Hölder norms of up :

                          lim sup k∇gp kLp + [gp ]0,αp < ∞ =⇒ H < ∞.
                           p→∞

Remark 2.6 (Parameter dependent rate). Theorem 1 is a straightforward consequence of the
more general statement Theorem 2 further down in Section 3.3 which asserts a convergence
rate, depending on a free parameter ε > 0. Optimizing over this parameter leads to the explicit
expressions in Theorem 1.
Example 2.1 (Lower bound). There is no reason to assume that our rates are sharp. Still,
the following example shows that the rate cannot be better than 1/p, not even locally. To
                                                         p−d
see this one considers the functions up (x) = |x| p−1 which solve (1.1) on the punctured ball
Ω := {x ∈ Rd : 0 < |x| < 1} with boundary values gp = 1 on the unit sphere and gp = 0 on the
center. The solution of (1.3) with the same boundary data g∞ = gp is given by u∞ (x) = |x|.
Since this is a radial problem we have

for t ∈ (0, 1). Hence, the maximum is attained in the interior. We observe that φ′ (t) = 0 is

   The lower bound of 1/p cannot be improved, even if one considers local convergence rates.
To see this, one can simply observe that
                                                  

Hence, for any smooth domain Ω′ which is compactly contained in Ω and contains the point
(1/2, 0, . . . , 0) one will have kup − u∞ kL∞ (Ω′ ) ∼ 1/p. Judging from this example one might
conjecture that the rate (at least for functions with positive gradient) is 1/p in general.

Remark 2.7. To obtain lower bounds for functions with vanishing gradient, which are expected
to be worse than 1/p a promising route might be to work with the p- and infinity-harmonic
functions which were implicitly constructed in [35, 37].


2.4    Extensions of our main result
Let us discuss some extensions of our results.
    We first note that the proof of Theorem 1 in Section 3 relies on only two properties of
p-harmonic functions: comparison with Hölder cones and Hölder regularity. Therefore, it is
straightforward to extend our result to other classes of PDE solutions which exhibit these
properties, and we give two examples in the sequel. Instead of p-harmonic functions, one could
be interested in harmonic function associated to the s-fractional infinity-Laplacian, introduced
in [18] (see also [7, 8]). For bounded and smooth functions u : Rd → R and s ∈ ( 12 , 1) it is
defined as
                        Z ∞
                            u(x + η v) − u(x − η v) − 2u(x)                      ∇u(x)
        (∆∞ )s u(x) :=                     1+2s
                                                            dη,     where v :=           .
                          0              η                                      |∇u(x)|

For ∇u(x) = 0 the definition has to be modified. Solutions us of the corresponding equations
                                (
                                  (∆∞ )s u = 0    in Ω,
                                                                                        (2.1)
                                  u = g∞          in Rd \ Ω,
                                                             2s−1
satisfy a comparison principle with the Hölder cones |x|    and are 2s − 1-Hölder continuous
if the boundary data g∞ are sufficiently regular [18, Section 3]. Therefore, in the proof of
Theorem 1 in Section 3.3 we can just plug α = β := 2s − 1 ∈ (0, 1) in (3.14) in order to obtain
the rate
                                                                           2s−1
                         kus − u∞ k∞ ≤ C(Ω, H, ku∞ k0,1 ) (1 − s) 4s ,

where, as before, u∞ denotes the solution of (1.3). Similarly, as for the p-Laplacian approxima-
tion discussed in Section 2.3 the rate asymptotically scales like (1 − s) /4 . Similar arguments
                                                                           1




                                                  6
can be performed for the so-called Hölder infinity Laplacian equation from [19] the solutions of
which also comparison with Hölder cones as well as Hölder regularity.
    Another extension of our results, albeit a less obvious one, concerns the convergence rate
of p-harmonic functions on a metric measure space (Ω, d, µ). Such functions are defined as
minimizers of a p-Dirichlet energy involving upper gradients, and admit a comparison principle
with respect to generalized Green functions. In the literature, the behavior of such Green
functions has mainly been investigated through capacitary estimates in the singular case (which
corresponds to p ≤ d in the Euclidean setting), see, for instance, [9, 11, 29]. Although the non-
singular case for large values of p should be easier to treat, to extend our results one would
need to prove the existence of a p-superharmonic Green function up (x, x0 ) with up (x, x0 ) = 0
which admits the following ratio convergence

                     supx∈B(x0 ,r) up (x, x0 )    1
                                                 − →0              as p → ∞, r → 0,
                     inf x6∈B(x0 ,2r) up (x, x0 ) 2

including quantitative estimates for the convergence above in terms of p, the Ahlfors dimension
of the measure, etc.


3    Proof of the main result
                                        
For x ∈ Rd and ε > 0 we let B(x; ε) := y ∈ Rd : |x − y| ≤ ε denote the closed ball of radius
ε around x. Furthermore, we let Ωε := {x ∈ Ω : inf y∈∂Ω |x − y| > ε} denote the inner parallel
set of Ω with distance ε to the boundary.
    In the following we let u : Ω → R be a function. We define upper and lower envelopes of u
as

                  uε (x) :=       sup      u(y),     uε (x) :=     inf      u(y),   x ∈ Ωε .            (3.1)

              S+ u(x) :=                  ,        S− u(x) :=                   ,         x ∈ Ωε .      (3.2)

A central tool for our techniques is the nonlocal (or finite difference) infinity-Laplacian which
is defined as

    We start by giving a brief outline of the proof strategy which relies on convenient proper-
ties of the nonlocal infinity-Laplacian ∆ε∞ as well as the comparison principle for p-harmonic
functions:



                                                       7
  1. Use established perturbation arguments to find w which satisfies
                            −∆ε∞ w ≥ δ 3 ,         |w − (u∞ )ε | . δ         in Ωε .

                                              −∆ε∞ uεp ≤ δ(ε, p)3
      for some δ = δ(ε, p) > 0 which also depends on the dimension d and the Hölder constant
      and exponent of up .
  3. Use step 1., step 2., an elementary comparison principle for ∆ε∞ , and flip the signs to
     conclude that
                          sup uεp − (u∞ )ε . δ(ε, p) + sup              uεp − (u∞ )ε .

      Use α-Hölder continuity to get
                                kup − u∞ k∞ . εα + δ(ε, p) + kgp − g∞ k∞ .

  4. Optimize over ε to obtain the final rate in terms of p.
Remark 3.1 (Alternative proof technique). We are thankful for a reviewer pointing out that
there might exist an alternative approach to proving convergence rates, based on the theory
of viscosity solutions. Such an approach would rely on perturbation statements for the usual
infinity-Laplacian ∆∞ (see Remarks 3.2 and 3.3 below) as well as the doubling-of-variables
technique. Since we believe that our approach generalizes easier to scenarios as in Section 2.4
and is, furthermore, more elementary, we refrain from going into more detail here.


3.1    Perturbations of infinity-harmonic functions
In this section we recall some important results which connect infinity-harmonic functions with
sub- and supersolutions of the operator ∆ε∞ . All results in this section were, to the best of our
knowledge, first proved in the PhD thesis [23] and picked up later, inter alia, in [4, 17, 22].
    We first recap the astonishing property of infinity-harmonic functions that their upper and
lower envelopes are sub- or supersolutions associated to the operator ∆ε∞ defined in (3.3).
The proof is almost trivial and solely relies on the comparison with cones property of infinity-
harmonic functions.
Proposition 3.1. Let u ∈ C(Ω) solve (1.3) Then it holds for all ε > 0 that
                                 −∆ε∞ uε ≤ 0 ≤ −∆ε∞ uε           in Ω2ε .                    (3.4)
Proof. The statement can be found in [23, Theorem 2.2.3] or [22, Lemma 5].
    The convenient property of the operator ∆ε∞ is that it admits a comparison principle of the
following form:
Proposition 3.2. Assume that for a constant C ≥ 0 the functions u, v : Ωε → R satisfy
                                          −∆ε∞ u ≤ C ≤ −∆ε∞ v                                (3.5)
in Ω2ε . Then it holds
                                    sup(u − v) = sup (u − v).                                (3.6)
                                     Ωε             Ωε \Ω2ε


                                                   8
Proof. The statement follows from [23, Theorem 2.6.5] or, more conveniently, from [17, Propo-
sition 3.3].
    In our final proof of convergence rates the role of u will be played by the upper envelope of
a p-harmonic function up which we will prove to satisfy −∆ε∞ uεp ≤ C, where C > 0 is a positive
constant that depends on ε, p, d, and the Hölder constants of u. So we need a comparison
function v which satisfies the inequality −∆ε∞ v ≥ C. Since according to Proposition 3.1 the
lower envelope of an infinity-harmonic function u∞ only satisfies −∆ε∞ (u∞ )ε ≥ 0 we need to
perturb it to a strict supersolution of this equation.
    This can be achieved using the following lemmas which state that one can perturb any
superharmonic function, associated to the operator −∆ε∞ , into a superharmonic function v
        ε
with S−   v bounded from below. Further, one can perturb any such v into a function w which
is a strict supersolution.
Lemma 3.1. If u : Ωε → R satisfies −∆ε∞ u ≥ 0 in Ω2ε , then for any δ > 0 there is a function
v : Ωε → R which satisfies

        −∆ε∞ v ≥ 0,         ε
                           S− v ≥ δ,     and       u ≤ v ≤ u + 2δ dist(·, Ωε \ Ω2ε )   in Ω2ε .

Proof. The proof can be found in a more general setting in [23, Lemma 2.6.3].
Remark 3.2 (Lemma 3.1 for ε = 0). As pointed out by a reviewer, there exists a corresponding
result for ε = 0 (cf. [17, (6.6)] or [24, Proposition 5.1]) the proof of which we sketch in the follow-
ing: Considering u which satisfies −∆∞ u ≥ 0 one defines Dδ := {x ∈ Ω : limε→0 Sε+ u(x) < δ}
which turns out to be an open set. Then one solves the eikonal equation

                           |∇û| = δ   in Dδ      with        û = u   on ∂Dδ

in the viscosity sense and sets
                                            (
                                             û    in Dδ
                                       v :=
                                             u     in Ω \ Dδ .

The function can be shown to satisfy −∆∞ v ≥ 0 and |∇v| ≥ δ in the viscosity sense and also
|u − v| ≤ Cδ for some domain-dependent constant C > 0.
    We note that the proof of Lemma 3.1 given in [23, Lemma 2.6.3] is a discrete version of the
above argument. Furthermore, as shown in the proof of [17, Theorem 2.19] one can combine
the result for ε = 0 with Proposition 3.1 to obtain yet another proof of Lemma 3.1.

Lemma 3.2. Suppose v : Ωε → R satisfies −∆ε∞ v ≥ 0 on Ω2ε . Then for all 0 ≤ δ ≤ 4kvk

3.2    Approximate consistency of p-harmonic functions
In this section we shall prove an approximate version of Proposition 3.1 for p-harmonic func-
tions. Since they do not admit comparison with cones, but rather comparison with Hölder
                      p−d
cones of the form |x| p−1 , their upper and lower envelopes are only approximate sub- and su-
persolutions.

3.3    Convergence rates
Now we have proved all we need for proving convergence rates. We first prove the following
convergence rate which depends on a free parameter ε > 0. Optimizing over this parameter
will then yield Theorem 1.
